slides.0.title: Diploma tasting and essays
slides.0.subtitle: Blind-tasting logic and essay skeletons
slides.1.title: Blind-tasting clues
slides.1.highlights.0.title: Pinot Noir
slides.1.highlights.0.content: Pale to medium ruby, red berries, fine tannin, high acidity: a richer Oregon wine may point to the Dundee Hills (Jory) or a hot year; a firmer, earthier one may suggest Yamhill-Carlton
slides.1.highlights.1.title: Washington reds
slides.1.highlights.1.content: Ripe fruit, medium-plus tannin, fairly high alcohol but retained acidity: Columbia Valley Cabernet, Merlot or Syrah; heat plus big day–night swings keep acidity
slides.1.highlights.2.title: Finger Lakes Riesling
slides.1.highlights.2.content: Green apple, lime, minerality and high acidity; dry to off-dry; low to medium alcohol
slides.1.content: Judge the climate first (cool, moderate, warm), then narrow to a region; do not guess the AVA first.
slides.2.title: Essay skeletons
slides.2.highlights.0.title: Structure
slides.2.highlights.0.content: Claim → natural conditions → human choices → style result → market and limits
slides.2.highlights.1.title: Sample prompt
slides.2.highlights.1.content: "Compare how the Willamette Valley and the Columbia Valley reach a balance of ripeness and acidity in different ways"
slides.2.highlights.2.title: Evidence
slides.2.highlights.2.content: Pair each claim with a dated fact, such as about 40 inches in the Willamette against about 6.2 in Horse Heaven Hills
slides.2.content: An essay is a chain of cause and effect, not a list of regions.
slides.3.title: Short-answer practice: question and marking points
slides.3.highlights.0.title: Question 1
slides.3.highlights.0.content: “Compare how the Willamette Valley and the Columbia Valley achieve the balance between ripeness and acidity in different ways.” (about 250 words)
slides.3.highlights.1.title: Marking points for question 1
slides.3.highlights.1.content: ① Willamette: maritime, about 40 inches of rain, rain-fed; cool → acidity kept naturally, the challenge is ripeness and vintage variation → Pinot Noir; ② Columbia Valley: rain-shadow desert, Horse Heaven Hills about 6.2 inches, irrigation needed; heat and diurnal range → reliable ripeness with retained acidity → Cabernet, Merlot, Syrah; ③ risks: autumn rain in Willamette, winter freeze in Columbia (1996, 2003); ④ conclusion: one “fights for ripeness”, the other “holds on to acidity”
slides.3.highlights.2.title: Question 2
slides.3.highlights.2.content: “Assess the impact of the 2005 Granholm v. Heald ruling on small and mid-sized US wineries.” (about 350 words)
slides.3.highlights.3.title: Marking points for question 2
slides.3.highlights.3.content: ① background: the post-Prohibition three-tier system (producer, wholesaler, retailer); ② ruling: states may not let in-state wineries ship direct while discriminating against out-of-state ones; the three-tier system itself remains lawful; ③ impact: small wineries can sell directly to consumers in other states (wine clubs, online), relying less on wholesalers, with small producers in Oregon, Washington, New York and elsewhere benefiting most; ④ limits: states can still impose permits, volume caps and tax rules, so compliance costs are high; ⑤ conclusion: it opened a channel but was not full liberalisation
slides.3.content: In comparisons cover both regions in every point; in assessments say what changed and what did not.
